federal.name: FAFSA (Free Application for Federal Student Aid)
federal.amount: The key to almost all need-based aid
federal.text: One free form decides your federal grants, work-study and loans, and most states and colleges use it for their own money too. The 2027-28 form (for students starting college in fall 2027) became available by October 1, 2026. The federal cutoff is June 30 at the end of the school year, but state and college deadlines come much earlier, some within weeks. File it as soon as you can.

federal.name: Federal Pell Grant
federal.text: Free money for undergraduates with financial need; it never has to be repaid. The amount depends on your Student Aid Index from the FAFSA, the cost of your college and whether you study full time. There is no separate application: filing the FAFSA is how you apply.

federal.name: Federal Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grant (FSEOG)
federal.text: Extra grant money for students with the greatest need. Each college gets a limited pot and hands it out until it runs dry, which is one more reason to file the FAFSA early. Not every college takes part.

federal.name: Federal Work-Study
federal.amount: A part-time job, paid at least minimum wage
federal.text: A campus or community job reserved for students with need, with hours built around your classes. You are paid directly and decide how to spend it. Tick the work-study box on the FAFSA to be considered.

federal.name: TEACH Grant
federal.text: For students who plan to teach a high-need subject in a low-income school. You must complete four years of that teaching within eight years of finishing your degree, or the grant turns into a loan with interest charged from the day it was paid. Take it only if you are sure about teaching.

federal.name: CSS Profile
federal.amount: Needed for many private colleges' own aid
federal.text: A second, more detailed aid form run by the College Board. Several hundred colleges, mostly private, require it before they will give their own grants, and those grants are often far larger than any outside scholarship. Check each college's aid page for whether it is required and by when.

search.name: CareerOneStop Scholarship Finder
search.text: Run by the U.S. Department of Labor. More than 9,500 scholarships, fellowships and grants, searchable by state, level of study and keyword. No account, no ads.

search.name: BigFuture Scholarship Search
search.text: The College Board's search. Free; uses the same account as the SAT and matches you to scholarships from your profile.

search.name: Fastweb
search.text: One of the oldest matching sites, with a large database. Free, but it needs an account and shows advertising; use a separate email address.

search.name: Scholarships.com
search.text: Large free directory you can browse by state, major and deadline without signing up.

search.name: Federal Student Aid Estimator
search.text: The government's calculator for how much federal aid you are likely to get, before you file the FAFSA.

search.name: How to spot a scholarship scam
search.text: The Department of Education's guide. The short version: you never have to pay to apply for a scholarship or to file the FAFSA, and nobody can guarantee you will win.
